case_patterns.title: Cloud kitchen start-up — launch financing and breakeven
case_patterns.business_context: Two founders in Karachi plan a cloud kitchen serving office districts through food-aggregator apps. They have Rs 8m of own savings and need Rs 12m more. The kitchen has no dine-in space; all orders come via aggregators charging 25% commission.
case_patterns.case_facts: Start-up needs Rs 20m total capital; founders contribute Rs 8m. Average order value Rs 900; food cost 32% of order value; aggregator commission 25%; delivery rider cost Rs 180 per order; monthly fixed costs (rent, salaries, utilities) Rs 1.1m. Founders project 4,000 orders/month in year 1. A bank offers a Rs 12m term loan at 22% for 4 years; an angel investor offers Rs 12m for 30% equity.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether the venture is viable and how the Rs 12m funding gap should be financed.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Dependence on aggregators; pricing power; scalability of the model.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Proceed with the launch, and choose between term debt and angel equity for the funding gap.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Sources of finance; breakeven analysis; contribution per order.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Total capital Rs 20m; founders Rs 8m; gap Rs 12m. Order economics: Rs 900 − food Rs 288 − commission Rs 225 − rider Rs 180 = contribution Rs 207/order. Fixed costs Rs 1.1m/month → breakeven ≈ 5,314 orders/month vs forecast 4,000.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Founders have restaurant operations experience but no delivery-logistics background; aggregator dependence gives limited pricing control.
case_patterns.missing_info: Customer acquisition cost; repeat-order rate; sensitivity of demand to delivery time.
case_patterns.constraints: Founders cannot contribute more than Rs 8m; loan requires personal guarantees; angel deal dilutes control.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Founders, angel investor, bank, aggregator platforms, riders, customers.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Bank term loan. 2) Angel equity. 3) Phased launch with one kitchen zone and lower fixed costs. 4) Do not proceed.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Breakeven feasibility; financing cost and risk; control implications; downside protection.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Textile spinning mill — declining margins
case_patterns.business_context: An established spinning mill in Faisalabad (30,000 spindles) has seen gross margin fall from 18% to 11% over three years while revenue is flat. Management blames cotton prices; the board suspects operational issues.
case_patterns.case_facts: Revenue flat at Rs 4.2bn for three years; gross margin 18% → 11%; operating expenses up 22%; energy cost per kg of yarn up 35%; waste percentage up from 4% to 6.5%; debtor days up from 52 to 71. Cotton prices rose 12% over the period while yarn prices rose only 5%. Two competitors maintained 15%+ margins.
case_patterns.main_issue: Diagnose the true drivers of margin decline and recommend corrective action.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Working capital deterioration; energy efficiency; competitor outperformance.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Which corrective actions to prioritise: cost programme, pricing action, or operational overhaul.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Ratio and trend analysis; variance analysis; root cause analysis.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Gross margin 18%→11% on flat Rs 4.2bn revenue (Rs 294m profit erosion). Opex +22%. Energy/kg +35%. Waste 4%→6.5%. Debtor days 52→71. Cotton +12% vs yarn price +5%.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Management attributes the decline to cotton prices; competitors held margins; maintenance backlog reported by plant staff.
case_patterns.missing_info: Competitor cost structures; age and efficiency of machinery; customer concentration.
case_patterns.constraints: Limited capex budget this year; unionised workforce; long-term cotton contracts expiring.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Operational turnaround (maintenance, waste reduction, energy). 2) Price increase push. 3) Product mix shift to finer counts. 4) Status quo with cost freeze.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Margin recovery potential; cash cost; implementation risk; time to impact.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Supermarket chain — new store investment appraisal
case_patterns.business_context: A Karachi-based supermarket chain (12 stores) considers opening a 13th store in DHA. Initial outlay Rs 180m (fit-out, equipment, initial stock net of supplier credit). Management forecasts incremental operating cash flows of Rs 38m p.a. for 8 years.
case_patterns.case_facts: Outlay Rs 180m at t=0. Forecast cash inflows Rs 38m p.a. years 1–8. Company WACC 16%. A pessimistic scenario (new competitor nearby) gives Rs 28m p.a.; optimistic Rs 46m p.a. Payback policy limit is 5 years. The site lease is 10 years with a 5-year break clause.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether the new store creates shareholder value.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Competitor entry risk; lease commitment; cannibalisation of the nearest existing store.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Approve or reject the Rs 180m store investment.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: NPV, IRR, payback; scenario analysis; capital rationing.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: NPV at 16%: Rs 38m × 4.3436 (8-yr annuity) = Rs 165.1m − Rs 180m = −Rs 14.9m. IRR ≈ 13.4%. Payback = 4.74 years. Pessimistic NPV ≈ −Rs 58m; optimistic ≈ +Rs 20m.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: DHA catchment is affluent and growing; nearest own store is 6 km away (limited cannibalisation); management has a strong store-opening track record.
case_patterns.missing_info: Probability of competitor entry; refurbishment capex in later years; terminal value of fit-out.
case_patterns.constraints: Capex budget allows only two of three proposed projects this year; 5-year payback policy.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Owners, store staff, suppliers, customers, landlord.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Open the store. 2) Reject. 3) Negotiate a shorter lease with break clause and re-appraise. 4) Smaller-format store at lower outlay.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: NPV; strategic fit; risk under competitor entry; payback discipline.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Intercity bus service — fare pricing decision
case_patterns.business_context: A Lahore-based intercity bus operator runs 40 coaches on the Lahore–Islamabad route. Load factor has slipped to 52%. A rival cut fares 15%; management considers matching the cut.
case_patterns.case_facts: Current fare Rs 2,200; variable cost per passenger Rs 700 (fuel share, tolls, refreshments); fixed cost per trip Rs 55,000; 55 seats per coach; 6 trips daily each way. Current load factor 52% (≈29 passengers). Rival fare Rs 1,870. Demand elasticity estimated at −1.4.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether to match the rival's 15% fare cut.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Service quality vs price competition; long-run cost structure.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Match the fare cut, hold fares, or reposition on service quality.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Contribution per passenger Rs 1,500 at current fare. Breakeven load ≈ 37 passengers (67%) per trip at current fare — current 29 passengers means trips run at a loss before allocated fixed costs. At rival fare Rs 1,870, contribution Rs 1,170; elasticity −1.4 implies demand rises ~21% to ~35 passengers — still below breakeven.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Brand is mid-market; on-time record is better than the rival's; staff fear a price war.
case_patterns.missing_info: Rival's cost position and staying power; customer price sensitivity by segment.
case_patterns.constraints: Fleet financing covenants require minimum debt-service cover; union agreements limit crew cuts.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Owners, passengers, staff, lenders, rival operator.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Match the fare cut. 2) Hold fares and invest in service differentiation. 3) Reduce frequency on weak departures. 4) Introduce off-peak discount fares only.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Trip-level contribution; cash flow vs covenants; competitive response risk.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: SaaS payroll start-up — pricing and Series A valuation
case_patterns.business_context: A Lahore SaaS start-up sells cloud payroll software to SMEs: 1,200 paying customers at Rs 8,000/month. It seeks Series A funding; investors propose a Rs 600m pre-money valuation. Annual recurring revenue is Rs 115m, growing 60% p.a.; gross margin 82%; monthly churn 3%.
case_patterns.case_facts: ARR Rs 115m; growth 60%; gross margin 82%; churn 3%/month; customer acquisition cost Rs 45,000; 1,200 customers. Burn Rs 9m/month; cash runway 8 months. Two valuation anchors: a DCF on forecast cash flows and revenue multiples of listed regional SaaS peers (8–12× ARR). Pricing is flat Rs 8,000/month regardless of headcount.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether the Rs 600m pre-money valuation is defensible and how pricing should evolve.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Cash runway; churn; tiered pricing opportunity.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Accept, reject or renegotiate the Series A terms; revise the pricing model.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: DCF valuation; revenue multiples; unit economics (LTV/CAC).
case_patterns.quantitative_info: LTV ≈ Rs 8,000 × 82% ÷ 3% ≈ Rs 218,667 per customer; CAC Rs 45,000 → LTV/CAC ≈ 4.9×. Peer multiples 8–12× ARR → Rs 920m–1,380m range, above the Rs 600m offer. Burn Rs 9m/month on 8 months runway.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Product is well-reviewed; the SME payroll market is under-penetrated; founder team is technical with no enterprise sales experience.
case_patterns.missing_info: Forecast cash flows for DCF; investor rights attached to the Rs 600m (liquidation preference, anti-dilution).
case_patterns.constraints: 8-month cash runway; founders want to keep majority control.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Founders, Series A investors, employees (ESOP), customers.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Accept Rs 600m pre-money. 2) Negotiate higher valuation with evidence. 3) Bridge round + pricing overhaul, raise later. 4) Tiered pricing now to lift ARR before raising.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Valuation defensibility; dilution and control; runway extension; pricing power.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Family-owned food processor — succession and dividend policy
case_patterns.business_context: A second-generation family food-processing company in Gujranwala (revenue Rs 1.8bn) faces the founder's retirement. Two siblings work in the business; a third wants dividends, not involvement. The company pays out 70% of profits as dividends and needs Rs 300m for plant modernisation.
case_patterns.case_facts: Profit after tax Rs 220m; dividend payout 70% (Rs 154m); retained Rs 66m p.a. Modernisation needs Rs 300m. Debt capacity limited by existing gearing of 55% (debt/equity). Sibling C (non-working) demands maintained dividends; siblings A and B want reinvestment and eventual buyout of C's 25% stake.
case_patterns.main_issue: Reconcile dividend expectations with the investment need and succession.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Valuation of C's stake; governance after the founder; dividend policy sustainability.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Set a sustainable dividend policy and a succession/buyout path.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Dividend policy and shareholder value; stakeholder conflict; financing choice.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Retained profits Rs 66m p.a. vs Rs 300m need → 4.5 years of internal funding at current payout. Cutting payout to 30% frees Rs 88m extra p.a. Gearing 55% limits debt.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Family harmony is at risk; the founder wants fairness but also business continuity; no formal shareholders' agreement exists.
case_patterns.missing_info: Fair value of C's 25% stake; tax implications of a buyout; willingness of A and B to guarantee debt.
case_patterns.constraints: No shareholder agreement; limited debt capacity; family expectations.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Founder, siblings A, B, C, employees, lenders.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Cut payout to 30% and fund modernisation internally. 2) Maintain payout and borrow (if capacity allows). 3) Buy out C's stake via phased payments. 4) Bring in an outside investor.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Family objectives; financial feasibility; fairness; business continuity.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Cement manufacturer — capacity expansion appraisal
case_patterns.business_context: A cement producer in the North zone runs at 94% capacity. Demand is forecast to grow 7% p.a. A new 1m-tonne line costs Rs 9bn, takes 2 years to build, and adds Rs 1.6bn annual operating cash flow from year 3 for 20 years. WACC 15%.
case_patterns.case_facts: Outlay Rs 9bn (Rs 5bn year 0, Rs 4bn year 1). Inflows Rs 1.6bn p.a. years 3–22. WACC 15%. Key risks: coal prices, a new competitor's announced plant, and PSDP (public development spending) volatility. Delaying one year preserves the option but risks losing market share.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether the Rs 9bn expansion creates value and when to commit.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Demand uncertainty; competitor capacity; construction risk.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Invest now, delay a year, or reject the expansion.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: NPV with phased outlays; sensitivity and scenario analysis; capacity planning.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: PV of outlays: Rs 5bn + Rs 4bn/1.15 = Rs 8.478bn. PV of inflows at 15%: Rs 1.6bn × annuity factor deferred 2 years ≈ Rs 1.6bn × 6.2593 × 0.7561 ≈ Rs 7.573bn. NPV ≈ −Rs 0.9bn (negative at 15%). Breakeven WACC ≈ 13.6%.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: North zone demand is historically cyclical; management has delivered past expansions on time.
case_patterns.missing_info: Competitor's actual construction timeline; long-run cement price assumptions.
case_patterns.constraints: Board requires NPV-positive at 15% hurdle; debt covenants cap gearing at 60%.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Shareholders, lenders, government (royalties), local community, competitors.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Invest now. 2) Delay one year and re-assess. 3) Smaller debottlenecking (Rs 2bn, +0.3m tonnes). 4) Reject.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: NPV at hurdle rate; sensitivity to coal prices and demand; strategic option value of waiting.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Auto parts maker — turnaround diagnosis
case_patterns.business_context: An auto parts manufacturer supplying two assemblers has posted two consecutive loss-making years. Revenue fell 18%; the company blames the auto sector downturn, but its market share also fell from 24% to 17%.
case_patterns.case_facts: Revenue −18% over two years; market share 24%→17%; operating loss Rs 180m last year; inventory days 96 (industry 55); defect rate 4.2% (contract limit 2%); key customer put the firm on watchlist. Fixed costs are 38% of sales. Debt/equity 1.8×.
case_patterns.main_issue: Distinguish sector-driven decline from firm-specific failure and design a turnaround.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Turnaround plan scope: operational fix, customer diversification, or orderly scale-down.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Root cause analysis; benchmarking; ratio analysis.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Revenue Rs 2.6bn (−18%); operating loss Rs 180m; inventory days 96 vs 55 industry; defect rate 4.2% vs 2% limit; fixed costs 38% of sales; D/E 1.8×.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Management blames the sector; the watchlist warning suggests customer confidence is the binding constraint.
case_patterns.missing_info: Order book visibility; competitor quality benchmarks; union stance on restructuring.
case_patterns.constraints: Customer watchlist; limited cash for capex; high leverage limits borrowing.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Two assembler customers, lenders, workers, suppliers, owners.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Quality-led turnaround with customer commitments. 2) Diversify into aftermarket parts. 3) Negotiated debt restructuring + cost programme. 4) Managed scale-down.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Customer retention; cash generation; feasibility; speed.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Fintech payments app — competitive pressure from a new entrant
case_patterns.business_context: A Karachi fintech's merchant-payments app (2m users) faces a deep-pocketed new entrant offering zero transaction fees for a year. The incumbent charges 1.5% per transaction and is not yet profitable.
case_patterns.case_facts: 2m registered users, 400k monthly actives; take rate 1.5%; gross margin 55%; monthly burn Rs 45m; runway 14 months. Entrant is backed by a regional super-app with 20m users. Switching costs for merchants are low; agent network is the incumbent's key asset (8,000 agents).
case_patterns.main_issue: How to respond to a zero-fee entrant without destroying unit economics.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Cash runway; agent loyalty; path to profitability.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Match on price, differentiate on service, seek a partner, or prepare for sale.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Competitive forces; portfolio/resource allocation; scenario planning.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Burn Rs 45m/month; runway 14 months. Matching zero fees on price-sensitive volume would cut revenue ~40% and halve runway. Agent network: 8,000 agents vs entrant's digital-only onboarding.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Merchants value the agent network for cash handling and trust; the entrant's subsidy is time-limited (one year).
case_patterns.missing_info: Entrant's post-promo pricing; investor appetite for a defensive funding round.
case_patterns.constraints: 14-month runway; cannot outspend the entrant on subsidies.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Founders, investors, merchants, agents, State Bank (regulator).
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Selective fee matching on at-risk merchants. 2) Double down on agent-led services. 3) White-label partnership with a bank. 4) Seek acquisition by the entrant.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Runway preservation; merchant retention; strategic value of the agent network.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Pharmaceutical plant — operational inefficiency and variances
case_patterns.business_context: A pharma formulation plant in Karachi missed its profit budget by Rs 95m. Material price variance is Rs 40m adverse; labour efficiency variance Rs 28m adverse; fixed overhead volume variance Rs 35m adverse on lower volumes.
case_patterns.case_facts: Budgeted profit Rs 320m; actual Rs 225m. Material price variance Rs 40m (A) — API prices rose after a supplier switch. Labour efficiency Rs 28m (A) — new hires, training gaps. Fixed overhead volume Rs 35m (A) — volumes 12% below budget after a DRAP pricing delay. Some variances overlap: cheaper API caused higher rejection rates.
case_patterns.main_issue: Separate controllable operational failures from planning (budget) errors and recommend fixes.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Which variances to investigate, what corrective action, and whether standards need revision.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Material, labour and overhead variances; planning vs operational variances; relevant costing.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Profit shortfall Rs 95m = 40 (A) material price + 28 (A) labour efficiency + 35 (A) fixed overhead volume, partly offset by Rs 8m favourable sales mix. Volumes 12% below budget.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: The cheaper API supplier caused higher rejections — the price saving created the efficiency loss. DRAP's pricing delay was outside management's control.
case_patterns.missing_info: Revised standard costs; supplier quality scorecards; training completion rates.
case_patterns.constraints: DRAP pricing approvals; GMP compliance limits on supplier switching speed.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Management, production staff, suppliers, DRAP, distributors.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Revert to the original API supplier. 2) Renegotiate with training investment. 3) Revise standards and budgets. 4) Combined corrective programme.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Controllability; net cost impact; GMP compliance; speed.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Listed manufacturer — debt vs equity financing decision
case_patterns.business_context: A listed engineering company needs Rs 1.5bn for a new plant. Options: a 5-year term loan at 20% or a rights issue at a discount. Current market cap Rs 6bn; debt Rs 1.2bn; tax rate 29%.
case_patterns.case_facts: Funding need Rs 1.5bn. Term loan at 20% pre-tax. Rights issue: 1-for-4 at 15% discount to market (TERP implications). Current D/E (market) 0.2. Cost of equity (CAPM): Rf 12%, beta 1.1, market return 18% → 18.6%. WACC currently ≈ 17.2%. Loan covenants: current ratio ≥ 1.2, dividend restriction if cover < 2×.
case_patterns.main_issue: Choose the financing route that minimises cost without endangering flexibility or shareholder wealth.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Dilution and TERP; covenant headroom; signalling.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Term loan, rights issue, or a mix.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: WACC; CAPM cost of equity; rights issues and TERP; capital structure.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: All-debt: D/E rises to 0.45; interest Rs 300m p.a.; after-tax cost 14.2%. Rights issue: ~Rs 1.5bn at discount dilutes ~21% of shares; TERP falls ~3.6%. WACC with debt ≈ 16.4% vs with equity ≈ 17.6% — debt is cheaper but adds risk.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Promoters hold 55% and will take up rights; the share price is depressed, making dilution expensive in value terms.
case_patterns.missing_info: Bank's final covenant package; issue costs of the rights offer; rating impact.
case_patterns.constraints: Covenant limits; promoter control threshold; market appetite for the issue.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Full term loan. 2) Full rights issue. 3) 50/50 mix. 4) Defer the plant.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Cost of capital; shareholder wealth (TERP); financial risk and covenants; control.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: FMCG distributor — working-capital crisis
case_patterns.business_context: A Peshawar-based FMCG distributor grew revenue 40% in a year but now cannot meet supplier payments. The overdraft (Rs 120m limit) is fully drawn; two suppliers have put the firm on cash-in-advance.
case_patterns.case_facts: Revenue Rs 1.4bn (+40%); receivable days 68 (up from 45); inventory days 52 (up from 38); payable days 30 (down from 41 as suppliers tightened). Cash conversion cycle 90 days vs 42 last year. Overdraft Rs 120m fully drawn at 24%. Net margin 3.1%.
case_patterns.main_issue: Restore liquidity without killing the growth.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Supplier confidence; credit discipline; profitability of growth.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Emergency working-capital plan: which levers, how much cash, how fast.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Cash conversion cycle; liquidity risk; receivables and inventory policy.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: CCC 90 days (68 + 52 − 30) vs 42 last year. Each 10 days of CCC ≈ Rs 38m cash tied up (Rs 1.4bn/365). Returning to 42 days releases ~Rs 184m. Overdraft cost 24% on Rs 120m = Rs 28.8m p.a.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Growth came from extending credit to new retailers; the sales team is incentivised on revenue, not collections.
case_patterns.missing_info: Aged debtor analysis; slow-moving inventory lines; supplier renegotiation room.
case_patterns.constraints: Suppliers on cash-in-advance; overdraft at limit; no unencumbered assets for more borrowing.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Owner, suppliers, retailers, bank, sales staff.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Aggressive collection + inventory cut + supplier renegotiation. 2) Factoring receivables. 3) Equity injection by owner. 4) Slow growth deliberately.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Cash released; speed; cost; damage to sales and supplier relations.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Furniture manufacturer — make-or-buy decision
case_patterns.business_context: A Sialkot furniture maker produces 20,000 chairs p.a. A supplier offers finished chair frames at Rs 2,400 each. In-house frame cost: materials Rs 1,100, labour Rs 700, variable overhead Rs 300, allocated fixed overhead Rs 600.
case_patterns.case_facts: In-house full cost Rs 2,700 vs supplier Rs 2,400. But Rs 400 of the Rs 600 allocated fixed overhead is unavoidable (depreciation, supervisor salary); Rs 200 is avoidable. Freed capacity could make tables contributing Rs 500 each; table demand would absorb 60% of freed frame-shop hours. Supplier quality is unproven; lead time 3 weeks vs 1 week in-house.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether outsourcing the frames actually saves money on a relevant-cost basis.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Quality and lead-time risk; use of freed capacity.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Make or buy the chair frames.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Relevant costing; opportunity cost; limiting factors.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Relevant in-house cost = 1,100 + 700 + 300 + 200 (avoidable fixed) = Rs 2,300 vs supplier Rs 2,400 → making saves Rs 100/frame before opportunity. Freed capacity: tables at Rs 500 contribution could add further benefit if demand exists for 60% of hours.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Supplier quality unproven; 3-week lead time vs 1 week in-house affects delivery promises.
case_patterns.missing_info: Supplier's financial stability; table demand beyond 60% of freed hours; redundancy costs.
case_patterns.constraints: Labour agreements limit layoffs; customer delivery commitments.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Continue making. 2) Outsource fully. 3) Outsource partially and use freed capacity for tables. 4) Renegotiate with the supplier on quality guarantees.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Relevant cost saving; quality and delivery risk; strategic capability.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Ceramics exporter — special order pricing
case_patterns.business_context: A Gujranwala ceramics maker (70% capacity utilisation) receives a one-off export enquiry for 50,000 tiles at Rs 380 each. Normal price Rs 520. Incremental cost Rs 330 per tile; the order needs no extra fixed cost but would use 25% of spare capacity.
case_patterns.case_facts: Normal price Rs 520; offer Rs 380; incremental cost Rs 330; contribution Rs 50/tile → Rs 2.5m total. Spare capacity 30%; order uses 25% of spare capacity. The buyer's market has 5% export rebate. Regular distributors must not learn of the price.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether to accept a below-normal-price export order.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Price leakage to regular customers; use of spare capacity; export rebate benefit.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Accept or reject the special order, and at what terms.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: Special order pricing; contribution; relevant cost.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Contribution Rs 50 × 50,000 = Rs 2.5m; plus 5% export rebate on Rs 19m = Rs 0.95m → total benefit ~Rs 3.45m. No opportunity cost (spare capacity).
case_patterns.qualitative_info: One-off buyer; no long-term relationship expected; confidentiality of the price is critical.
case_patterns.missing_info: Probability of price leakage; alternative uses of spare capacity next quarter.
case_patterns.constraints: Spare capacity is 30%; the order consumes most of it; delivery schedule is tight.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Management, regular distributors, workers (overtime avoided), the export buyer.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Accept at Rs 380. 2) Counter at Rs 420. 3) Reject. 4) Accept with confidentiality and non-repeat clauses.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Incremental profit; leakage risk; capacity opportunity cost.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Textile exporter — foreign exchange risk and hedging
case_patterns.business_context: A Karachi garment exporter invoices USD 3m quarterly, receivable in 90 days. The rupee has swung 8% in a quarter before. Finance is debating whether to hedge and with what.
case_patterns.case_facts: Exposure USD 3m per quarter, 90-day terms. Spot Rs 278/USD. 90-day forward Rs 281.5. A 90-day currency option (strike 280) costs 1.8% of notional. Money-market hedge possible via USD borrowing. Last year an unhedged 6% adverse move cost Rs 46m. Hedging policy does not exist; the board wants one.
case_patterns.main_issue: Design an FX hedging policy: whether, how much and with which instruments.
case_patterns.secondary_issues: Cost of hedging vs volatility; speculation vs hedging discipline.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Adopt a hedging policy (instrument, hedge ratio, governance).
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: FX hedging instruments; money market hedge; risk management process.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Forward locks Rs 844.5m (3m × 281.5). Option costs ~Rs 15m (1.8% × 834m) for downside protection with upside retained. A 6% adverse move ≈ Rs 50m exposure. Money-market hedge: borrow USD now, convert, invest PKR — effective rate depends on interest differential.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: No hedging policy exists; treasury has limited derivatives experience; the board is risk-averse after last year's loss.
case_patterns.missing_info: Forecast accuracy of USD receipts; bank credit lines for margin; tax treatment of hedge gains/losses.
case_patterns.constraints: Limited treasury expertise; SBP regulations on derivatives use.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Full forward cover. 2) Options for 50% + forwards for 50%. 3) Money-market hedge. 4) Remain unhedged with a stop-loss policy.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Certainty of cash flows; hedging cost; flexibility; governance.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper

case_patterns.title: Acquisition of a packaging company — valuation and deal appraisal
case_patterns.business_context: A listed food company considers acquiring a flexible-packaging supplier (its largest vendor) for vertical integration. Asking price Rs 1.1bn. Target: revenue Rs 900m, EBITDA Rs 180m, net debt Rs 250m.
case_patterns.case_facts: Asking price Rs 1.1bn (equity). Target EBITDA Rs 180m; net debt Rs 250m → implied EV Rs 1.35bn = 7.5× EBITDA. Listed packaging peers trade at 6–8× EBITDA. DCF (WACC 16%, 4% terminal growth) gives EV Rs 1.15bn. Synergies: Rs 40m p.a. procurement and logistics savings. 60% of target revenue comes from the acquirer itself.
case_patterns.main_issue: Whether Rs 1.1bn is a fair price and the deal creates value.
case_patterns.decision_to_make: Bid, negotiate down, or walk away.
case_patterns.relevant_concepts: EV vs equity value; DCF; multiples; synergy valuation.
case_patterns.quantitative_info: Implied EV 7.5× EBITDA vs peers 6–8× (top of range). DCF EV Rs 1.15bn → equity Rs 900m, below asking. PV of Rs 40m synergies at 16% ≈ Rs 250m+ → with synergies, value to acquirer ≈ Rs 1.15bn equity.
case_patterns.qualitative_info: Vertical integration secures supply; the target's customer concentration (60% from acquirer) cuts both ways — captive demand but integration risk.
case_patterns.missing_info: Quality of earnings; capex needs; management retention; tax attributes.
case_patterns.constraints: Board walk-away: no deal above 8× EBITDA EV; funding via debt within covenant limits.
case_patterns.stakeholders: Acquirer shareholders, target owners, lenders, employees, customers.
case_patterns.alternatives: 1) Bid Rs 1.1bn. 2) Bid Rs 950m anchored on DCF. 3) Structured deal (earn-out on synergies). 4) Walk away and tender supply competitively.
case_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Value creation vs asking price; synergy achievability; concentration risk.
case_patterns.source_basis: Original practice case authored for this application — not an ICAP past paper
